prompt: Which principal grants a role to every member of a team, as the team changes?
hint: Joining and leaving happen in the directory.

choices.text: `user:planner-devs@example.com`
choices.why: `user:` names one account. A group's address with the wrong prefix names nobody useful.

choices.text: `group:planner-devs@example.com`
choices.why: Right. Membership is read at the moment of the request, so the policy never has to change.

choices.text: `domain:example.com`
choices.why: That is every account in the company, not the team.

choices.text: `allAuthenticatedUsers`
choices.why: That is every Google account in the world.

choices.text: Every account in the company's own domain
choices.why: That is `domain:example.com`. This one has no domain in it.

choices.text: Every principal that already holds a role in the project
choices.why: It is not limited to the project. It reaches beyond the company altogether.

choices.text: Service accounts only, since people sign in differently
choices.why: People and programs alike are included, as long as they hold a Google identity.

choices.text: Any Google account in the world, a new Gmail one included
choices.why: Right. It sounds careful and is not: signing in is all it asks.

prompt: A developer leaves. With roles granted to groups, what has to change?

choices.text: Only their membership of the groups, in the directory
choices.why: Right. Every role ends with it, and no IAM policy is touched.

choices.text: Every policy that names one of those groups
choices.why: The policies name the group, which still exists; only who is in it changed.

choices.text: The groups themselves, which must be deleted and recreated
choices.why: The group outlives any of its members. Deleting it would end everybody's roles.

choices.text: Nothing until the account is deleted in Google Cloud
choices.why: Accounts live in the directory, not in Google Cloud.

prompt: A colleague tries to grant `user:ana.personal@gmail.com` a role in production and is refused, though they hold the right role. What refused it?
hint: Lesson 4 has a guardrail about whose accounts may be granted roles.

choices.text: Gmail accounts cannot hold Google Cloud roles
choices.why: They can, in an estate with no such guardrail. This one has one.

choices.text: The directory, which suspended Ana's personal account
choices.why: A company's directory does not hold personal Gmail accounts at all.

choices.text: A domain restriction, from lesson 4
choices.why: Right. `iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains` refuses any account outside the listed domains.

choices.text: The production folder's location policy
choices.why: A location policy is about places, not people.

hint: Read the address from the right.

choices.text: The default Compute Engine account
choices.why: That one is named after the project number, at `developer.gserviceaccount.com`.

choices.text: Pub/Sub's service agent
choices.why: A service agent's name starts with `service-` and the project number.

choices.text: An account somebody created in `planner-dev`
choices.why: Right. NAME@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com is the form of the ones you create.

choices.text: A person whose address ends in `gserviceaccount.com`
choices.why: Nobody signs in as a person at that domain; it is where service accounts live.

prompt: Why one service account per workload, rather than one shared by the reports job and the website?
hint: What does a shared account hold?

choices.text: Each would hold all of the other's roles
choices.why: Right. Separate accounts keep each workload's roles, and its blast radius, its own.

choices.text: A service account can only be attached to one machine
choices.why: One account can be attached to many machines. That is exactly the risk.

choices.text: Google bills each service account separately
choices.why: Service accounts cost nothing; the reason is about permissions.

choices.text: Quotas are counted per service account
choices.why: Quotas are counted per project, mostly. The reason is the roles.

prompt: In an organisation created in 2021, a machine was created without naming a service account. What does it run as, and what was the risk?

choices.text: No account at all, so it cannot call any API
choices.why: A machine with no account named gets the default one.

choices.text: Pub/Sub's service agent, with Pub/Sub roles only
choices.why: Service agents act for Google's services, never as a machine's identity.

choices.text: The account of whoever created it
choices.why: A machine never runs as a person.

choices.text: The default account, holding Editor
choices.why: Right. Older organisations granted it Editor automatically, so every such machine could edit everything.

prompt: A policy contains `deleted:serviceAccount:reports@planner-dev.iam.gserviceaccount.com?uid=104729...`. A new account named `reports` is created in the same project. Does it hold the old roles?

choices.text: Yes: the name matches, and IAM grants by name
choices.why: That is exactly what the `deleted:` rewrite and the uid exist to prevent.

choices.text: No: the grant is pinned to the old account's uid
choices.why: Right. The uid stops an old grant from coming back to life under a reused name.

choices.text: Yes, but only for thirty days
choices.why: There is no grace period; the new account starts with nothing.

choices.text: It cannot be created while the deleted entry exists
choices.why: The name can be reused. Only the old grants stay with the old account.

prompt: Match each service account to who created it.
hint: Look at the domain after the `@`.

pairs.right: Compute Engine, when the API was enabled
Pub/Sub, for its own work in the project

prompt: What is the difference between a workforce pool and a workload pool?

choices.text: Workforce is for people, workload is for programs
choices.why: Right. A workforce pool lives on the organisation; a workload pool lives in a project.

choices.text: Workforce is for Google accounts, workload for service accounts
choices.why: Both pools are for identities from outside Google, which is the point of federation.

choices.text: They are the same pool in two consoles
choices.why: They are two different resources, at two different levels of the tree.

choices.text: Workload pools are paid and workforce pools are free
choices.why: The difference is who the identities are, not the price.

hint: What does an address alone not say?

choices.text: `example.com` is not a real domain
choices.why: The provider cannot know which domains are real; it checked only the form.

choices.text: Viewer cannot be granted on a project
choices.why: With `user:` in front, the same grant planned without complaint.

choices.text: It has no prefix, and IAM never guesses the kind
choices.why: Right. It could be a person or a group, and IAM will not guess.

choices.text: Google refused the placeholder token
choices.why: `validate` sends nothing to Google.

prompt: Which principal grants a role to every CI job whose token says it came from the repository `example/planner`, and to no other?
hint: A set, chosen by an attribute of the token.

choices.text: `principal://.../workloadIdentityPools/ci-pool/subject/example/planner`
choices.why: `principal://` names one subject, and a subject is a single job's identity, not a repository.

choices.text: `principalSet://.../workloadIdentityPools/ci-pool/attribute.repository/example/planner`
choices.why: Right. A principalSet picks every identity of the pool whose attribute has that value.

choices.text: `group:example/planner`
choices.why: `group:` names a Google group by address. A repository is not one.

choices.text: `serviceAccount:example-planner@planner-dev.iam.gserviceaccount.com`
choices.why: That is a service account inside Google Cloud, not the outside jobs.

prompt: `grants.tf` uses `for_each` over a map of principals. How many grants does the plan add?
hint: One per entry of the map.

prompt: The plan for the five grants passes. Why would every one of them still be refused if applied?
hint: A plan checks form. What does Google check?

choices.text: Viewer may not be granted to five principals at once
choices.why: A role may be granted to any number of principals.

choices.text: `for_each` resources are applied one per day
choices.why: Terraform applies them together, in one run.

choices.text: A project may not grant roles to a domain
choices.why: `domain:` is a valid principal on a project.

choices.text: Google checks a principal exists, and these do not
choices.why: Right. The provider checks how a principal is written; Google checks that it is real.

prompt: The planner team needs: the developers to read production, the reports job to read one bucket, and GitHub Actions in `example/planner` to deploy. Which principals fit, in that order?
hint: A group, a service account, a set from a pool.

choices.text: `user:` for each developer, `serviceAccount:`, `group:`
choices.why: Grants per person rot when people leave, and a CI system is not a Google group.

choices.text: `domain:`, `allAuthenticatedUsers`, `serviceAccount:`
choices.why: `domain:` is the whole company, and `allAuthenticatedUsers` for a job is a public grant.

choices.text: `group:`, the default Compute Engine account, a downloaded key
choices.why: The default account is shared by every machine, and a key is a credential, not a principal.

choices.text: `group:`, `serviceAccount:`, `principalSet://`
choices.why: Right. A group for the people, an account of its own for the job, and a pool's set for the outside CI.
